text: Yes. I just unmuted myself. Thank you for the opportunity. And yes, I am speaking as a resident of Hunter's Hill and a long-term resident of Hunter's Hill. It's a place that I've provided community input for the last 45 years and both in local government and through community leadership and engagement. Hunter's Hill community doesn't take lightly the issue of heritage. And it's one of the defining issues of our community. It is one of those attributes that make our community unique. And we can't apply rules that appear in other councils to Hunter's Hill readily. Hunter's Hill is driven by that uniqueness from a heritage point of view, from a landscape point of view, from a whole range of aspects. And it's that community and the community's understanding of those attributes that I'm here to represent today. There's a long history with managing heritage in Hunter's Hill. And one of those important aspects is transparency and engagement with the community. Since the development of, or introduction of LPPs, that is now by ministerial directive, empowered in four people that are present at those meetings. I think that transparency and public discourse and public opportunity to engage with that process is critical for an area like Hunter's Hill. And it needs to be retained at the LPP level for that reason. Another issue I have concern with is the term minor. There's no definition of it in the proposal. And my view of heritage, which as I say is a long standing engagement, is that heritage is not facadism. It is about the whole. And quite often at the Conservation Advisory Panel, we talk about looking at the whole of the property, not just what it looks like from the street, which a lot of people would like us to do. Elements within that property, whether it's a fireplace, whether it's an addition to the back and how that fits into the proposed development, I think are quite crucial. And people see that from different lenses. And that's where the value is in the LPP being the custodian of those decisions.

For example, we've had a situation with the council chambers where important aspects of heritage have now the potential to be lost because of an advice or an interpretation of what is heritage by council and its staff. speaker: jimsanderson
text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak, Mr. Chair. I reflect a lot of the things that Councillor Williams has said. First point I'll make is that as a councillor, I'm very conscious that I should not or I've got to abide by the decisions of the elected body of council. Unfortunately, this proposal has not gone through the elected body of council, which I find so disappointing. I accept that the panel should not be bothered with very minor items. So I differ from Councillor Williams very slightly in that respect. But I would start by referring to the Borough Charter. And this applies so much to Hunter's Hill where the Borough Charter in its preamble states that places of cultural significance, rich people's lives, often providing deep and inspirational sense of connection to community and to landscape, to the past lived experiences, their historic records that are important expressions of the Australian identity and experience. Places of culture and significance reflect the diversity of our communities, telling us about who we are and the past that has formed us and the Australian landscape. This statement is incredibly applicable. It's almost as though it was designed for Hunter's Hill. The Borough Charter goes on to define cultural significance embodied in the place itself, its fabric, settings, use, association, meanings, records, related places and related objects. Fabric means all the physical material in places including elements, fixtures, contents and objects. Elements that contribute to most, to cultural or natural significance of heritage items will vary greatly from one item to another. So significant analysis may be required before it is even possible to understand whether works will impact or the impact of works will be minor. The principle weakness of the proposal is that the delegation does not define what minor is and it leaves the same person to make that assessment as to do the ultimate decision as to whether the application will proceed. The other, what needs to happen if we're going to have any form of delegation, we must need to define precisely. And I expected the sort of definitions I could think of will only be of things of a very minor nature like a minor tree pruning or whatever. And the other thing I'll make a point on, I know that this covers the, which is covered in the wording of the delegation, but it's incredibly important that any delegation that is provided cannot allow development that would otherwise come within the municipal planning's direction on the 23rd of February, 2018, which set out various thresholds as to which development should come within the scope of determination by the local planning panel. I therefore recommend that the panel defer decision on this if we're going to delegate at all, so that we can precisely define what it is that might be regarded as minor. I would certainly accept something like minor pruning of a tree or whatever. I don't think the panel needs to be bothered with that sort of detail. But at the same time, I think we need far greater protection of the heritage, which is just so important to this community. Thank you.
